extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulatory policy analysts, and government officials involved in designing or evaluating regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for governments on applying stakeholder engagement, regulatory impact assessment, and ex post evaluation to make evidence-based, effective regulation. Focuses on when and how to consult, assess impacts, consider alternatives, and review rules after adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders, based on their lived experiences, can provide valuable input on the feasibility and practical implications of regulations; providing members of the public the opportunity to help shape, challenge, and reform rules is important for improving the design and implementation of those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engagement helps create buy-in, build trust in government, strengthen democratic values, and encourage higher compliance, especially when stakeholders feel policymakers considered their views. OECD highlights stakeholder engagement as one of three core tools for improving regulatory outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult at early stages of policy making
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer than one-quarter of OECD countries systematically consult citizens and businesses at early stages of policy making to gather data and ideas on potential policy solutions; early-stage input is exactly when it can make the biggest difference in identifying appropriate policy options and ensuring rules work in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should systematically consult early to identify feasible policy options, ensure practicality, and secure buy-in. Early engagement is more likely to influence choice of approaches and prevent design problems than late-stage consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide public responses to consultation comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Around three-fifths of policymakers do not provide public responses to comments received during consultations, leaving stakeholders unsure whether and to what extent their input shaped resultant rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public responses/feedback are important so stakeholders understand how their input was used; lack of feedback may dissuade future participation. Best practice is to acknowledge, summarize, and explain how comments affected decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) to inform decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory impact assessment supports decision making by providing objective information about the likely benefits and costs of policy proposals; a well-functioning RIA system promotes policy effectiveness, efficiency, and coherence by illustrating trade-offs within regulatory proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIAs should objectively assess benefits and costs, reveal trade-offs and unintended consequences (e.g., reducing risks in one area may create risks in another), and help avoid regulatory failures. RIAs are a core tool OECD recommends for evidence-based policy making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensively consider all feasible alternatives, including non-regulatory options
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers should comprehensively consider all feasible alternatives when developing proposals and consider solutions that avoid creating new laws or regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not predominantly emphasize the preferred regulatory approach vis-à-vis alternatives or consider only one non-regulatory option. Requiring consideration of alternatives but only analysing one risks embedding a perception that regulation is always warranted; best practice is to assess multiple reasonable options, including doing nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden impact assessment beyond economic factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries have broadened the range of impacts they consider, yet they still tend to consider more economic factors (such as impacts on competition and budget) than non-economic ones (such as gender equality, environmental, or social impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers must look at all relevant impacts—economic and non-economic—to understand potential effects of any proposed rule. RIAs and policy development should explicitly include gender, environmental, social, and other non-monetary impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct ex post evaluations / reviews of adopted rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After countries adopt new rules, ex post evaluations can help ensure they continue to work and can improve future regulations; all rules are experiments and governments rely on imperfect information to make rules that change behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex post reviews enable course correction when rules fail and help adapt rules as contexts change. OECD provides best practice principles for reviewing a country's stock of regulations; reviews should be designed to build on successes and learn from mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically assess whether rules are working; avoid 'set-and-forget'
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer than one-quarter of OECD member countries systematically assess whether rules are working as intended, meaning many governments never review a large number of rules and a 'set-and-forget' mentality still prevails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish systematic processes and schedules for ex post review so regulations are periodically reassessed for effectiveness, relevance, and unintended consequences. Use reviews to ensure regulations continue to maximize community well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reviews as a vehicle for improvement and learning (especially after crises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries are not currently using reviews as a vehicle for improvement or learning; given the depth and breadth of rules introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic, reviews will be central for governments to understand what has worked and what has not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reviews to extract lessons from rapid or emergency rule-making, to rejuvenate and realign regulations, and to prepare better for future crises. Treat reviews as active improvement tools rather than mere compliance checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and scale online consultations where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation on draft laws is relatively well established and governments have increasingly undertaken consultations online, a change accelerated with the COVID-19 pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online consultations can expand reach and accessibility, but should be structured to ensure meaningful input, avoid piecemeal engagement, and be paired with practices (e.g., public responses) that sustain participation.
